worked_examples.text: Se mann gedǣlde ðæt sǣd fram ðǣm gærse.
worked_examples.translation: The man separated the seed from the grass.
worked_examples.learner_block:
**Se mann gedǣlde ðæt sǣd fram ðǣm gærse.** — The man separated the seed from the grass.

The thing separated, **ðæt sǣd**, is accusative; **ðǣm gærse** is dative after **fram**. These are particular constructions. They do not establish one case rule for all spatial prepositions.
worked_examples.scope_note: New composition using checked construction and lexemes. Preserve the earlier light/darkness specific-passage adaptation and locator as history, not as a citation for this exact new wording. Only singular grass is used.

worked_examples.learner_block:
**Ðā hwalas sindon dēor.** — The whales are animals.

Both subject **hwalas** and predicate **dēor** are nominative plural; the neuter plural **dēor** has no added ending.
worked_examples.scope_note: Nominative plural predicate dēor has zero ending. Does not print the singular COMP04 answer.

worked_examples.learner_block:
**on ðæs fugles trēowe** — in the bird's tree

**Trēowe** is dative after locative **on**; **ðæs fugles** remains genitive. **Ðæs** agrees with **fugles**, not with **trēowe**.

reading_support.exact_table_row: | **ofer ðǣre nēowolnesse brādnesse** | **Ofer** means “over” and here requires a dative head. Apply the nested-genitive construction of §9 to identify the head and its dependent. |

Here **ofer** has accusative plural **wæteru**, unlike the preceding dative construction. |

reading_support.exact_table_row: | **cwæð ðā** | “Then said”: **cwæð** is third-person singular preterite; this **ðā** is the adverb “then,” not the article. |

reading_support.exact_table_row: | **lēoht wearð geworht** | “Light was made/came into being.” **Wearð** is a third-person singular preterite used here with past participle **geworht** in a passive phrase. |

reading_support.exact_table_row: | **geseah ðā ðæt hit gōd wæs** | “Then saw that it was good.” **Geseah** is third-person singular preterite; **ðā** is “then”; **ðæt** is the conjunction “that.” **Gōd** is a neuter nominative singular predicate adjective. The copula stands at the end of the embedded clause. Use the context and §8 for the reference of **hit**. |

reading_support.exact_table_row: | **hē gedǣlde** | **Gedǣlde** is “separated,” third-person singular preterite. Identify the reference of the subject pronoun from the preceding clause. The object and **fram** phrase use §9. |

reading_support.expression: hēt ðæt lēoht Dæg, and ðā ðīestru Niht
reading_support.exact_table_row: | **hēt ðæt lēoht Dæg, and ðā ðīestru Niht** | “[He] called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” **Hēt** is third-person singular preterite, with God/he understood as subject. **Ðæt lēoht** and **ðā ðīestru** are accusative objects; **Dæg** and **Niht** are accusative names applied to them. Here **ðæt** and **ðā** are articles. |
reading_support.remaining_learner_decision: Complete naming construction/analysis and understood God/he supplied; ordinary accusative recognition does not establish independent naming production.

reading_support.expression: Ðā wæs geworden ǣfen and morgen ān dæg.
reading_support.exact_table_row: | **Ðā wæs geworden ǣfen and morgen ān dæg.** | “Then there came to be evening and morning: one day.” **Wæs geworden** expresses a resulting state or completed coming-to-be, “had come to be”; **geworden** is a past participle. **Ān dæg** is “one day,” not the ordinal “first day.” Treat this closing formula as a whole. |
reading_support.remaining_learner_decision: Whole formula and one-not-first meaning supplied; no unique syntax or generalized agreement required.
